title: Letters to the Heads of State • The Killing of Abu Rafi‘ • Final Word • Practical Resolve

blocks.0: Letters to the Heads of State
blocks.1: The Treaty of Hudaybiyah brought a safe time. The Prophet {{1}} used that time; he wrote letters to Kisra, Qaysar, the Najashi and every powerful ruler around, calling them to Allah.
blocks.3: As soon as letters came up, the Companions said, the rulers of Rome do not read any letter without a seal. The Prophet {{1}} then had a silver ring made. Anas (RA) said, I can still seem to see its white gleam in the Prophet’s {{2}} hand.
blocks.5: I can still seem to see its white gleam in the hand of the Prophet {{1}}; its design was ‘Muhammad Rasul Allah’.{{2}}
blocks.6: The design was in three lines. Above ‘Muhammad’, in the middle ‘Rasul’, below ‘Allah’. And the Prophet {{1}} had said that no one else should make this design. Reaching the rulers in the very manner in which they read letters. Taking into account the etiquette of the one being called. We often take speaking in our own way as honesty. If we first think in what language, in what manner the one who will listen understands, the word reaches.{{2}}
blocks.8: To al-Muqawqis, the ruler of Egypt, Hatib ibn Abi Balta‘ah (RA) took the letter. In the letter the same call: accept Islam, you will be safe; Allah will give you double reward. Hatib (RA) said to al-Muqawqis, before you in this Egypt there was a man who thought himself the great lord. Allah seized him in both places, this world and the Hereafter. Take a lesson from another’s end; let not others take lesson from your end. al-Muqawqis said, we too have a religion. We will not leave it unless we find something better. Hatib (RA) said, I call you to Islam. As on Musa’s lips was the good news of ‘Isa’s coming, on ‘Isa’s lips was the good news of this Prophet. We are not asking you to turn away from the Christian religion; we call you to a more complete path. al-Muqawqis thought for a long time. Then he said, I have thought about this Prophet. I have seen that he does not call to anything disliked, nor forbid anything liked. He is not an impostor, nor a soothsayer. He gives true news of hidden matters, he foretells. I will think more. He kept the letter carefully in an ivory box, sealed it and gave it into a maidservant’s hand. Then he called a scribe who knew how to write Arabic and had a reply written. In the reply was, I knew that a prophet was yet to come, but I thought he would come from Syria. I have honoured your envoy. I am sending for you two maidservants of great honour among the Copts, some cloth and a mule for riding. al-Muqawqis did not advance even one step beyond this. He did not accept Islam.{{1}}
blocks.9: We often take courteous behaviour as consent. When someone speaks with a smile, sends a gift, honours the envoy, we think, he agrees. al-Muqawqis did everything: he thought, he honoured, he sent gifts. But he did not move from his place. Courtesy and decision are not the same thing. Even within a good reply there can be a ‘no’.
blocks.10: Abu Sufyan in the Court of Heraclius
blocks.11: Heraclius, the emperor of Rome, was then in Sham. When the letter arrived he enquired whether anyone from this man’s land was nearby. At that time Abu Sufyan was in Sham with a trade caravan of Quraysh, not yet a Muslim. He was called to the court.{{1}}
blocks.12: Heraclius said, which of you is the closest relative of this man? Abu Sufyan said, I. He seated him in front, his companions behind him; he told them, if he lies, you will point it out. Abu Sufyan used to say later, if not for the shame of being known as a liar, that day I would have lied about him. Then question after question. How is his lineage? High lineage. Has anyone among you made such a claim before? No. Was any of his forefathers a king? No. Who follows him, the influential or the weak? The weak. Are his followers increasing or decreasing? Increasing. Does anyone turn back resentful toward this religion after accepting it? No. Before the claim, did you ever accuse him of lying? No. Does he break promises? No; now we are in a term of a treaty with him, we do not know what he will do in it. Abu Sufyan used to say, apart from this one sentence I found no chance to insert anything anywhere else. Have you fought him? Yes. What was the result? Sometimes he wins, sometimes we. What does he tell you to do? He says, worship Allah alone, associate no one with Him, give up what your fathers used to say; pray, speak the truth, be chaste, maintain kinship.{{1}}
blocks.13: The man who was then one of the Prophet’s {{1}} greatest enemies, who even had the wish to lie, from his own mouth that day, in the enemy’s court, came the testimony of prophethood. Such is the force of truth; even the one who wants to suppress it, it makes open his mouth.
blocks.14: And ‘Does he break promises? No.’ This answer came right in the middle of the Treaty of Hudaybiyah, the treaty in which Abu Jandal had to be returned. The witness to keeping the word that day was the enemy’s own mouth.
blocks.16: Having heard everything Heraclius explained one by one. Prophets come from just such lineage; if it were a royal line it could be said, he wants a lost kingdom; the man who does not lie to people will not lie about Allah; the followers of prophets are the weak; faith grows exactly like this, once it sits in the heart it does not leave; prophets do not betray. Then he said, if what you say is true, he will become owner even of this place under my two feet. I knew he would come; but I did not think he would come from among you.{{1}}
blocks.17: The letter was read out. A short letter, every word measured and placed.
blocks.19: Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. From Muhammad, servant of Allah and His Messenger, to Heraclius, the ruler of Rome. Peace upon whoever follows guidance. Now then, I call you with the call of Islam. Accept Islam, you will be safe; Allah will give you double reward. And if you turn away, the sin of your subjects too will fall upon you.{{1}}
blocks.20: At the end of the letter was a verse of Surah Al ‘Imran; the call to that common word of the People of the Book, worship of none but Allah alone. No threat, no entreaty; a clear proposal and its consequence. As soon as the reading of the letter ended an uproar rose in the court, Abu Sufyan and his men were thrown out. Coming out, Abu Sufyan said to his companions, the affair of Ibn Abi Kabshah has become very big; even the king of Banu al-Asfar fears him. He used to say, from that day I was certain he would be victorious; in the end Allah put Islam into my heart.{{1}}
blocks.21: Heraclius recognised the truth, but drew back out of fear of losing kingship. Abu Sufyan accepted nothing that day, but the seed had been sown. Recognising the truth is one thing, the courage to accept it another.
blocks.23: A letter went to Kisra, the emperor of Persia, too. ‘Abdullah ibn Hudhafah al-Sahmi (RA) took the letter. He had been told to give it into the hand of the ruler of Bahrain; he delivered it to Kisra. Kisra read it and tore the letter into pieces. Hearing the news the Prophet {{1}} made du‘a that they too be torn completely to shreds.{{2}}
blocks.24: There is a report of what happened next. A Persian man came to the Prophet {{1}}. The Prophet {{2}} said to him, my Lord has killed your lord, that is Kisra, tonight. ‘My Lord’ means Allah. ‘Your lord’ means Kisra, whom the man took as lord. The Prophet’s {{3}} Lord is one. He was also informed that Kisra had made his daughter his successor. He said,
blocks.26: A people that makes a woman its ruler never succeeds.{{1}}
blocks.27: The treasures too the Prophet {{1}} had spoken of, in another hadith of Sahih al-Bukhari: when Kisra is destroyed there is no Kisra after him, when Qaysar is destroyed there is no Qaysar after him; and their treasures will certainly be spent in the way of Allah.{{2}}
blocks.28: The one who tore the letter, his empire was in fact torn to shreds before two decades had passed. To insult a call that comes with respect is really to tear one’s own fate. In anger we too tear up letters received, throw away advice received. But if what was written in the letter was true, tearing does not change the truth.{{1}}
blocks.30: To al-Mundhir ibn Sawa, the ruler of Bahrain, al-‘Ala’ ibn al-Hadrami (RA) took the letter. al-Mundhir read the letter out to all the people of Bahrain. Many were glad and accepted Islam, many disliked it and moved away. al-Mundhir wrote, in my area there are fire-worshippers and Jews too; let me know your view about them. The Prophet {{1}} wrote the reply, I have accepted your recommendation about your people. Leave those who have accepted Islam on their Islam. I have forgiven the offenders, accept that from them. As long as you remain on the path of peace and good, you will not be removed from your post. And whoever of the Jews or fire-worshippers wants to remain in his religion must pay the jizyah. To Hawdhah ibn ‘Ali, the ruler of Yamamah, Salit ibn ‘Amr (RA) took the letter. The word of the letter was, my religion will soon reach as far as the hoof of the camel or the horse can reach. Accept Islam, you will be safe; your kingdom will remain yours. Hawdhah gave Salit the honour of a royal guest. After reading the letter, going neither right nor left, he wrote a middling reply, the path you call to is very beautiful. The Arabs fear me; give me some responsibility, I will follow you. The Prophet {{2}}, hearing the reply, said, even if he asks for a piece of land, I will not give it to him. He will perish himself, and what is in his hand will perish too.{{3}}
blocks.31: al-Mundhir and Hawdhah both received the same call. One read it out to everyone; the other wanted to bargain. Faith is not a thing to be shared out. We often put even the truth up for price. Let this much right be mine, let that much be conceded, then I will accept. But the truth that is accepted only on conditions is no longer the accepting of truth, it is dressing one’s own interest in the mask of truth.
blocks.33: To al-Harith ibn Abi Shimr, the Ghassanid ruler of Damascus, Shuja‘ ibn Wahb al-Asadi (RA) took the letter. In the letter was, believe in Allah alone, who has no partner; your kingdom will remain yours. al-Harith threw the letter far away. He said arrogantly, who will snatch my kingdom from me? I will set out against him right now. He asked the emperor of Rome for permission to fight the Prophet {{1}}. Qaysar stopped him. al-Harith sent Shuja‘ ibn Wahb (RA) off with clothes and expenses.{{2}}
blocks.34: Fear of losing kingship and the promise of protecting kingship; both were in the same letter. The language of the letter was soft. But to an arrogant mind even soft words feel like fire. We measure others’ words with our own fear. The man who is saying, it will be good for you, in fear and suspicion we hear, he wants to remove me.
blocks.36: The Prophet {{1}} sent a small group of the Ansar to the Jew Abu Rafi‘. The leader of the group was ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Atik (RA). Abu Rafi‘ used to hurt the Prophet {{2}} and help his enemies against him. He lived in a fortress of the Hijaz. The sun had set. The people were returning home with livestock. ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Atik said to his companions, you sit here. I will go and try to get in by some stratagem with the gatekeeper. Going near the gate of the fortress he sat covering his head with his cloth, as if relieving himself. The gatekeeper called, servant of Allah, if you want to enter, enter, I will close the gate. He went in and hid. Everyone entered, the gate was closed. The gatekeeper hung the bunch of keys on a peg. ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Atik went and took the key, and opened the gate. Abu Rafi‘’s night gathering sat on the upper floor. The gathering broke up. He went upstairs. He would open one door, bolt it from inside; then another. He thought, even if people notice they will not be able to catch me before I reach Abu Rafi‘. A dark room. Abu Rafi‘ in the middle of the family. In which corner, impossible to tell. He called, Abu Rafi‘! A reply came, who? He struck toward the voice. It did not work. Abu Rafi‘ cried out. He came out. After a while, changing his voice, he entered again and asked, what is that noise, Abu Rafi‘? He said, woe to your mother! Someone in the room struck me with a sword. ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Atik struck again; still it was not finished. Then he set the tip of the sword in the belly and pressed, it went to the back. He understood the job was done. He began going down opening the doors one after another. Reaching near the stairs he thought he had reached the ground. He put his foot down. A moonlit night. He fell. The shin of his leg broke. He took off his turban and bound the leg. Then he walked and sat near the gate. He said, I will not go out tonight until I am sure I have killed him. The rooster crowed. On the fortress wall a herald stood and announced, I announce the death of Abu Rafi‘, the merchant of the Hijaz. Only then did he return to his companions. He said, hurry, Allah has finished Abu Rafi‘. Reaching the Prophet {{3}} he told it all. The Prophet {{4}} said,
blocks.38: Stretch out your leg. I stretched out my leg. He wiped it; as if nothing had ever happened to me.{{1}}
blocks.40: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Atik could have fled. His leg broken, the night deep. But he sat until the sure news came in the herald’s voice. We often spread news on mere hearsay; even before the rooster crows. He sat on his broken leg only to make one matter firm. And coming back with the broken leg he went first to the Prophet {{1}}. News of the work, news of the pain, both to be taken to the one to whom they should be taken. That leg was healed by his touch.
blocks.42: Some pictures stay fixed in the mind from this journey of Hudaybiyah. A she-camel sitting down at Hudaybiyah, and right after it the declaration, I will accept any proposal in which the sanctities of Allah are honoured. Fourteen hundred hands under the tree, the vow not to flee up to death. Erasing ‘Rasul Allah’ from his own name, because it takes nothing away from prophethood. Abu Jandal in chains, and a prophet forced to return him, who did not break his word. ‘Umar’s question and Abu Bakr’s exactly identical answer. A crisis passed by one counsel of Umm Salamah. And in the court of Heraclius the testimony in the enemy’s mouth; he does not break promises. One hiding under the camel’s belly beneath the tree, and the Prophet’s {{1}} hand stretched out on behalf of the absent ‘Uthman. The surah that descended on the way back, whose name is ‘Victory’, for the journey many thought a defeat. The signet ring for Rome. The three commanders who came out of Quraysh’s house, one of whom had said, how much longer? The letter kept in al-Muqawqis’s ivory box and the consent withheld. Hawdhah’s bargaining and al-Harith’s thrown-away letter. An Ansari who waited on a broken leg for the rooster to crow. The word which, if kept, brings loss, if broken no one will ever know; the test is exactly there. So take one deed home from today’s dars.
blocks.44: Abu Jandal in chains had to be returned, yet the Prophet {{1}} did not break the word given. Today I will ask myself a question: in the matter where keeping my word would cost me and breaking it no one would ever know, what do I do? Today I will keep one promise which, if broken, no one would have said anything; I will not give up this habit of keeping a word given from today.

footnotes.0: Sahih Muslim 2092 (from Anas (RA): ‘when the Prophet {{1}} wished to write to Rome, the Companions said, they do not read any letter without a seal; so he had a silver ring made… its design was “Muhammad Rasul Allah”’). Sahih al-Bukhari 3106, 5878 (Anas: the design was in three lines, ‘Muhammad’ one line, ‘Rasul’ one line, ‘Allah’ one line). Sahih al-Bukhari 5877 (the Prophet {{2}} said, I have had a ring made, had it engraved ‘Muhammad Rasul Allah’; let no one make this design). The making of the seal was in the period after the treaty; the sahih hadith gives no definite mention of the time; the beginning of sending letters is in this period, Al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 571–572 and Ibn al-Qayyim, Zad al-Ma‘ad 3/60.
footnotes.1: Sahih Muslim 1774 (from Anas (RA): ‘the Prophet {{1}} wrote letters to Kisra, Qaysar, the Najashi and every powerful ruler, calling them to Allah’). In one narration there is an extra sentence, ‘this Najashi is not that Najashi whose funeral prayer the Prophet {{2}} prayed’; in another narration the sentence is absent. Al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 574–578: there is disagreement about the letter to the Najashi; some think it was the letter of the time of the first hijrah to Habashah (in the hand of Ja‘far (RA)), some that it was written to Ashamah, some to his successor. In this dars the Najashi’s reaction is not told.
footnotes.2: Sirah-based: Al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 578–580 (Ibn al-Qayyim, Zad al-Ma‘ad 3/61 also mentions this letter). Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence. Muqawqis is a title; the name is disputed among the Sirah scholars (Juraij ibn Matta, according to others Binyamin; al-Rahiq, p. 578, note 568). Hatib ibn Abi Balta‘ah (RA) was the envoy. The two maidservants of the gift were named Mariyah and Sirin; in Mariyah’s house Ibrahim was later born, Sirin the Prophet {{1}} gave to Hassan ibn Thabit (RA) (al-Rahiq, p. 580). That Muqawqis did not accept Islam is also in al-Rahiq.
footnotes.3: Sahih al-Bukhari 7 (from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Abbas (RA), Abu Sufyan’s own narration). The event was during the term of the Treaty of Hudaybiyah, Abu Sufyan himself told it.
footnotes.4: Part of the same Sahih al-Bukhari 7 (question and answer).
footnotes.5: Part of the same Sahih al-Bukhari 7 (Heraclius’s analysis and remarks).
footnotes.6: Sahih al-Bukhari 7 (the text of the Prophet’s {{1}} letter). At the end of the letter Surah Al ‘Imran 3:64 is quoted.
footnotes.7: The end part of the same Sahih al-Bukhari 7. ‘Ibn Abi Kabshah’ is a contemptuous nickname the polytheists used for the Prophet {{1}}; ‘Banu al-Asfar’ is a name for the Romans.
footnotes.8: Sahih al-Bukhari 4424, 64, 7264 (from ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Abbas (RA)): the Prophet {{1}} sent his letter to Kisra with ‘Abdullah ibn Hudhafah al-Sahmi (RA); he instructed him to give it into the hand of the ruler of Bahrain; he delivered it to Kisra; Kisra read it and tore it. Ibn al-Musayyib says, the Prophet {{2}} then made du‘a against them that they be torn completely to shreds (there is a word of doubt of the kind ‘I think Ibn al-Musayyib said’ on the narrator’s part, so the du‘a part rests on the narrator’s impression).
footnotes.9: Musnad Ahmad 20438 (from Abu Bakrah (RA); Shu‘ayb al-Arna’ut: sahih): ‘a Persian man came to the Prophet {{1}}; he said: inna rabbi qad qatala rabbaka, ya‘ni Kisra (my Lord has killed your lord, that is, Kisra). And he was informed that Kisra had made his daughter successor; then he said, a people that makes a woman ruler never succeeds.’ That the speaker is the Prophet {{2}} is clear in another sahih narration: from Dihyah al-Kalbi (RA) ‘go to your companion, tell him, my Lord has killed his lord, Kisra, tonight’ (Sahih al-Jami‘ 862, al-Albani: sahih), also ‘you two tell your companion’ (Silsilah Sahihah 1429). In the text of Ahmad the subject of the word ‘faqala’ is not linguistically clear; in this dars, on the basis of the parallel sahih narrations, the speaker is taken to be the Prophet {{3}} (in al-Wadi‘i’s Sahih Dala’il al-Nubuwwah 177 the same statement with the words ‘rabbi tabaraka wa ta‘ala’; the commentaries have not examined this question separately). The hadith gives no date for when Kisra was killed.
footnotes.10: Sahih al-Bukhari 3121 (from Jabir ibn Samurah (RA)): ‘when Kisra is destroyed there is no Kisra after him, when Qaysar is destroyed there is no Qaysar after him; by the One in whose hand is my soul, their treasures will certainly be spent in the way of Allah.’ It is in Sahih Muslim too. The hadith gives no date for when it was said.
footnotes.11: How many days it took for Kisra’s empire to break is not numbered in the hadith; ‘before two decades had passed’ is a calculation: Hudaybiyah was 6 AH, and the fall of the Persian empire was in ‘Umar (RA)’s time, in the early 20s of the Hijri years (Nihawand 21 AH, by the reckoning of history books), that is, in under twenty years.
footnotes.12: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 586–589 (Bahrain: al-Mundhir ibn Sawa and al-‘Ala’ ibn al-Hadrami; Yamamah: Hawdhah ibn ‘Ali and Salit ibn ‘Amr al-‘Amiri; Ibn al-Qayyim, Zad al-Ma‘ad 3/61–63). Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence.
footnotes.13: Sirah-based: al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (Bengali), pp. 589–590 (al-Harith ibn Abi Shimr al-Ghassani and Shuja‘ ibn Wahb al-Asadi; Ibn al-Qayyim, Zad al-Ma‘ad 3/63). Sirah-based; the chain has not been verified in this dars, so it has come as a scene, not as evidence. The incident of ‘Amr ibn al-‘As (RA)’s embassy to Jayfar and ‘Abd ibn al-Julandi of Oman has been called by al-Rahiq al-Makhtum (pp. 590–594) an event after the conquest of Makkah, so it has been kept outside this dars’s boundary.
footnotes.14: Sahih al-Bukhari 4039 (from al-Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA); ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Atik’s own words: ‘I reached the Prophet {{1}} and informed him, he said, stretch out your leg…’).
footnotes.15: Sahih al-Bukhari 4039, 4038 (from al-Bara’ ibn ‘Azib (RA)): the Prophet {{1}} sent several of the Ansar to Abu Rafi‘ the Jew, the leader of the group ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Atik; Abu Rafi‘ ‘used to hurt the Prophet {{2}} and help against him’, lived in a fortress of the Hijaz. The fortress gate, the bunch of keys, the doors one after another inside, the blow recognising the voice in the dark, the leg broken while going down, bound with a turban, ‘the rooster crowed, then a herald stood on the wall and announced: I announce the death of Abu Rafi‘, the merchant of the Hijaz’, reaching his companions ‘hurry, Allah has killed Abu Rafi‘’, telling it to the Prophet {{3}}, ‘stretch out your leg’, wiping it, ‘as if he had never been ill’. The Bukhari text does not mention the year; there is disagreement among Sirah scholars about the year of the event. According to the index the event of this dars; the Abu Rafi‘ of the fortress at Khaybar (Sallam ibn Abi al-Huqayq) and the Abu Rafi‘ of dars 15 (the Prophet’s {{4}} slave) are not the same person.

quiz.q: Why was Abu Sufyan in Sham at the court of Heraclius?
o: As a prisoner of war in Roman hands
quiz.e: He was in Sham with a trade caravan of Quraysh.

quiz.q: What did Kisra do on receiving the Prophet’s ﷺ letter?
o: Wrote a reply and sent it
quiz.e: He read the letter and tore it up.

quiz.q: When wanting to write to Rome, what did the Companions say?
o: They cannot read Arabic at all
They do not read a letter without a seal
They will not accept any letter at all
They only listen to the envoy’s spoken word, not writing

quiz.q: Which Companion took the letter to Kisra?
Which ruler sent honour and gifts in reply to the letter but did not accept Islam?
quiz.e: al-Muqawqis honoured the envoy Hatib, sent maidservants and gifts, did not change his religion.

quiz.q: Who demanded a share of ruling power in return for accepting Islam?
o: al-Harith ibn Abi Shimr of Ghassan
quiz.e: The Prophet ﷺ said, even if he asks for a piece of land I will not give it.

quiz.q: Why does the answer to ‘Does he break promises?’ get special importance in this dars?
o: Abu Sufyan had told an outright lie here
The answer came during the term of the Treaty of Hudaybiyah
Heraclius did not ask the question
It was part of the letter
quiz.e: This testimony in the enemy’s mouth came during that very treaty in which Abu Jandal was returned.

quiz.q: From the incident of the seal, what etiquette of da‘wah is understood?
o: Following the customs of the one being called
Sending an envoy instead of a letter
quiz.e: The rulers of Rome do not read a letter without a seal.

quiz.q: If someone insultingly throws away our letter or call, what is our responsibility, according to this dars?
o: To stop sending letters of da‘wah and withdraw
To deliver the call; the result is in Allah’s hand
quiz.e: Delivering the call is the duty; Kisra’s end was his own.

quiz.q: From which incident does the lesson of following the culture’s rules of the one being invited come?
o: Showing the sacrificial animals to the chief of Kinanah
The silver ring with a seal for Rome
quiz.e: The rulers of Rome do not read a letter without a seal (Muslim 2092).

quiz.q: The mistake of taking courteous behaviour and gifts as consent fits which incident?
quiz.e: Courtesy and decision are not the same thing.

quiz.q: ‘Let this much right be mine, then I will accept the truth’; which incident fits this bargaining?
o: Hawdhah’s asking for a share of power
quiz.e: The truth accepted only on conditions is no longer the accepting of truth.

quiz.q: Who was the leader of the Ansari group sent to Abu Rafi‘?
Why did ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Atik wait near the fortress gate on a broken leg?
o: Waiting for the leg to heal
Waiting for the gatekeeper to sleep
To be sure of the death news
quiz.e: When the herald announced the death he set out.

quiz.q: Which lesson of avoiding spreading news without certainty is in this dars?
o: Waiting for news on a broken leg
quiz.e: ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Atik did not set out until the news was made firm in the herald’s mouth.
